issues.legal_issue: The evidence supported the forgery convictions and the conviction for abetting forgery.
material_facts: The sale deed purported to convey land belonging to a person who had died years earlier, and the second accused impersonated that person to execute it.
The first accused participated in arranging the transaction and assisted the forgery; the second accused executed the forged deed.
The High Court found both accused guilty of forgery-related offences, although it acquitted the first accused on a procedural ground.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court sustained the second accused’s conviction for forgery and convicted the first accused of abetting forgery, setting aside his acquittal on that charge.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 467 and 114 of the Indian Penal Code, forgery of a valuable security and abetment of that forgery are punishable offences. When an appellate court agrees with the trial court’s view of the evidence, it need not repeat the evidence or the reasons already given; Girija Nandini Devi v. Bigendra Nandini Choudry was relied on for that approach.

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_forgery_convic: The proceeding is an appeal asking a court to review convictions for forgery-related conduct.
predicates.evidence_establishes_forgery: The evidence establishes that a document was forged.
predicates.evidence_establishes_each_accused_role: The evidence establishes each accused’s role in committing or abetting the forgery.

issues.definition: When an appeal reviews forgery convictions and the evidence establishes the forgery and each accused’s role, the convictions are sustained.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement for a court complaint does not bar a private prosecution for forgery and abetment when the forged document was never introduced in the related court proceeding.
material_facts: A forged sale deed was registered before the redemption suit was filed.
The private complainant initiated the criminal complaint after learning of the deed.
The forged deed was never produced in evidence at any stage of the redemption suit.
The prosecution alleged both forgery-related offences and an offence of fabricating false evidence.
issues.conclusion: The restriction in Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply to the alleged offence under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code because the deed was never produced in the suit. The private complaint could therefore proceed for forgery and abetment, and the first accused could be convicted of abetment of forgery. The Magistrate could not take cognizance of the Section 193 offence in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires a written complaint by a court for specified offences, including offences under Sections 193 to 196 of the Indian Penal Code, when alleged to have been committed in or in relation to a court proceeding. The Court approved the principle in In re V. V. L. Narasimhamurthy that, when a single transaction includes both an offence requiring a court complaint and an offence not requiring one, prosecution cannot be split to proceed on only the latter. But that principle did not bar prosecution here because the deed was never put in evidence and the alleged Section 193 offence was not within the restriction. The Court also relied on Patel Laljibhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat and Raghunath v. State of U.P. concerning the scope of the court-complaint restriction.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_based_on_private_co: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution initiated on a private complaint.
predicates.alleged_false_evidence_involves_a_court_: The prosecution alleges that false evidence was fabricated for use in, or in relation to, a court proceeding.
predicates.forged_document_never_introduced_in_that: The forged document was not produced or given in evidence at any stage of the related court proceeding.

issues.definition: A private prosecution for forgery or abetment is not barred when it includes an allegation of false evidence connected to a court proceeding but the forged document was never introduced there.

issues.legal_issue: The restriction on private prosecution for specified offences committed by a party to a court proceeding does not extend to an offence committed before that person became a party.
material_facts: The sale deed was forged and registered before the redemption suit was filed.
The prosecution concerned the earlier forgery and abetment, rather than a forged document created after the accused had become a party to the suit.
issues.conclusion: The restriction in Section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not extend to specified offences committed by a person before becoming a party to the proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Patel Laljibhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat held that the words concerning an offence committed by a party to a proceeding refer to an offence committed in the person’s character as a party, after becoming a party. Raghunath v. State of U.P. followed that principle. The Court explained that the restriction protects the administration of justice and is confined to offences with a sufficiently close nexus to the proceeding.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_concerns_an_offence: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution for an offence whose private prosecution is restricted when committed by a party to a court proceeding.
predicates.offence_committed_before_accused_became_: The accused committed the alleged offence before becoming a party to the relevant court proceeding.

issues.definition: The party-status restriction does not bar private prosecution when the relevant offence was committed before the accused became a party to the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not interfere with a sufficiently reasoned reduction of sentence for an accused whose role and circumstances support leniency.
material_facts: The second accused was found guilty of forgery but was described as illiterate and as having put her thumb impression on the deed when asked to do so by the other accused.
The High Court found that she had forged the document independently, but considered her circumstances and reduced her sentence.
The State appealed against the reduced sentence, and the Supreme Court found the High Court had given sufficient reasons for taking a lenient view.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the reduced sentence imposed on the second accused.
issues.legal_principle: The appellate court may decline to interfere with a reduced sentence where the lower appellate court has given sufficient reasons for leniency. The Court applied that principle to its review of the sentence for the offence under Section 467 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: state_appeal_challenges_reduced_sentence and conviction_remains_in_force and offender_circumstances_support_leniency and lower_appellate_court_gave_sufficient_reasons

predicates.state_appeal_challenges_reduced_sentence: The proceeding is a state appeal challenging a sentence reduced on appeal.
predicates.conviction_remains_in_force: The accused’s conviction remains in force.
predicates.offender_circumstances_support_leniency: The offender’s circumstances and role provide grounds for a lenient sentence.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_gave_sufficient_re: The lower appellate court explained why it reduced the sentence.

issues.definition: A reduced sentence is not disturbed when the conviction remains in force, the offender’s circumstances support leniency, and the lower appellate court gave sufficient reasons.
